Read the complete One Piece card code

The character name is a starting point, not a unique printing. Keep the letters, numbers and separator in the printed card code. Searching only the last digits can mix records from different releases.

  1. Find the full code on the card. Copy the set prefix and card number together.
  2. Compare the printed card type, artwork and frame with the candidate. A character can appear on a Leader card and on other cards.
  3. Check the language and visible finish on your physical copy.
  4. Compare the result with the official One Piece Card Game card list when you need a publisher reference.
  5. Open the matching catalog record for its available price source and observation date.

If the code is unclear, enlarge the card image or inspect the card directly. Enter the part you can read and compare the candidates. Do not fill an uncertain digit with the number from a convenient search result.

Compare standard, alternate and manga artwork

Alternate artwork can share a printed card number with a standard version. The number can therefore identify a card without settling which artwork you own. Compare the whole illustration, background, character pose and frame with the candidate image.

Treat a seller's description such as “alternate” or “manga” as a detail to check. A cropped listing image can hide information needed to identify the version. Use the full card front, then confirm the exact artwork on the selected record.

Inspect the physical finish separately. Glare can obscure artwork in a photo, while colored light can alter the apparent surface. Use even light and a straight-on view. If two records remain plausible, search the full code and compare them before choosing a price.

Keep Leaders, parallels and product printings distinct

A shared character name does not make two cards interchangeable. Match the printed type and code before comparing a Leader, another card featuring that character, or a different product printing. Keep any visible product marking or stamp in the comparison.

When the artwork and number match but a listing names another product, check the release and marking instead of assuming it is the same copy. Store the confirmed printing as its own holding in the app. Quantity belongs to that printing, rather than to every card with the character's name.

Verify the language on the actual card

Compare the language of the printed text with the catalog record. A seller's listing language or your browser's translation does not change the language of the physical card. Japanese and English copies need their own matching records and price context where available.

Language shown on one record does not establish coverage for every release in that language. If the exact code, artwork and language are absent, keep the identification unresolved. Do not substitute an English record for a Japanese copy, or apply another finish's price.

Recover from a wrong or missing match

  • Only standard artwork appears: search the full code in the One Piece catalog, then compare the available artwork records.
  • The character is right but the card type differs: return to the printed type and full code. A matching name alone is insufficient.
  • The photograph is hard to read: retake one card front with the borders visible. Keep other cards and packaging out of the crop.
  • The record exists without a price: use its identity details, but leave the amount unavailable. Missing data is not a zero value.

Check a price before adding your copy

Use the card price checker to understand the source, currency and observation date. A raw-card reference does not price an existing slab unless the selected price series matches that grading company and grade.

For app holdings, record the confirmed printing, quantity and raw condition or existing slab grade. Collection reference totals use available published prices. They are separate from the cards' purchase costs and from an amount a buyer may offer.

One Piece card scanner questions.

Can CardScanFox tell alternate art from the standard printing?

The scan suggests likely records, but alternate art can share a card number with the standard version. Review the artwork and confirm the correct record before adding or pricing it.

Does it work on Japanese One Piece cards?

Match the language printed on your card to the catalog record. Japanese and English copies use separate matching records and price context where available; one language field does not prove complete release coverage.

Can I track One Piece alongside other games?

Yes. The iPhone app can organize confirmed One Piece holdings alongside other supported games. Its reference total uses available published prices; website scan results do not add holdings to that collection.

Can I check One Piece card prices without the card in hand?

Yes. Search for the exact One Piece printing without a photo, then check the available price and its date. Confirmed holdings contribute to a reference total using available published prices. Missing prices remain unavailable; the total is not a live transaction feed or guaranteed sale amount.
